resolved_title: Can Interdistrict Choice Boost Student Achievement? The Case of Connecticut's Interdistrict Magnet School Program
notes: Abstract only (crossref); no full text. Kraft's rows (grade 8, n 514 to 516, ES 0.25 and 0.11) match the lottery-based sample of applicants to interdistrict magnet middle schools; lottery samples of applicants code universal with opt_in 1 per codebook section 2. The abstract states no achievement or characteristic rule for applicants; 'central city students' describes the sample rather than an eligibility rule. WWC sample text ('students in both urban and suburban settings') adds nothing on eligibility. Abstract capped at medium confidence.

evidence_quote: The headline findings are based on all pupils in both groups who reported in the pre-test survey before randomisation that they would like to be involved in something like CU (henceforth the 'volunteers').
resolved_title: Children's University: Evaluation report and executive summary (EEF, December 2017)
notes: EEF school-randomised trial, 68 primary schools in the north of England, Years 5 and 6 (aged 9 to 11); international setting. All pupils in the year cohorts were surveyed; the analytic sample is those who said they would volunteer for CU-type activities, so opt_in 1 with no achievement or characteristic rule. Schools were recruited from areas with low existing CU provision, not on need (tie-breaker 6). Kraft's four effects match executive summary Table 1 (p. 5): 0.12 reading and 0.15 maths are the volunteer sample (n 1,224 and 1,231); 0.03 reading and 0.05 maths are the EverFSM subgroup (n 493 and 494), which on its own would be targeted_other. Coded on the full volunteer sample per tie-breaker 5 with mixed_samples 1.

evidence_quote: Before the start of each new school year, schools sent us lists of students whom they wanted placed into one of the classes in an identified randomization block, and we randomly assigned these students to classes.
resolved_title: Supplying Disadvantaged Schools with Effective Teachers: Experimental Evidence on Secondary Math Teachers from Teach For America (Mathematica Working Paper 31, Chiang, Clark, and McConnell, May 2014)
notes: Document mismatch: text/168-clark-2013.txt is the 2014 TFA-only working paper, a companion to the cited Clark et al. (2013) IES report on TFA and Teaching Fellows; the Teaching Fellows sample is excluded from it (footnote 8, p. 11). Kraft's row (grades 6 to 12, n 12,699, ES 0.00) does not match the working paper's 5,790 randomized students and 0.07 SD effect, and the 0.00 likely comes from the Teaching Fellows analysis or a pooled figure, hence mixed_samples 1 and confidence capped at medium. School rule, same page: 'Eligible schools were those with sets of TFA and comparison teachers teaching math classes that could form a randomization block for the study.' Sample rule in both halves: districts with many TFA (or TF) math teachers, schools with a TFA and a comparison teacher on the same course, all students the school placed in those classes randomized between them; no achievement or characteristic criterion. The WWC sample text for the Teaching Fellows half describes the same design (classroom matches, students randomly assigned within matches). Schools are highly disadvantaged (about 80 percent FRL, p. 16) but were not chosen on that trait.
